content: We have that S_5 is not solvable: docs#Equiv.Perm.not_isSolvable_fin_5. Do we have that S_4 is solvable? We need this for CGT, since it implies a field which is quadratically and cubically closed is also quartically closed.
Hmm, looks like a Mathlib API gap to me
Would having the statement that every group of order <60 is solvable be worth having in mathlib? (even though the proof would kind of need to go through all cases and use general statements)
@loogle Equiv.Perm, commutator
:search: alternatingGroup.commutator_perm_eq, alternatingGroup.commutator_perm_le, and 3 more
I'm surprised the three key theorems assume the unnecessary condition 5 ≤ Nat.card α

To reduce to the alternating group, you can use docs#alternatingGroup.commutator_perm_le
For n<=3, you can use docs#alternatingGroup.isMulCommutative_of_card_le_three
For n=4, you can use docs#alternatingGroup.kleinFour_eq_commutator and docs#IsKleinFour.isMulCommutative

Felix Pernegger said:

Would having the statement that every group of order <60 is solvable be worth having in mathlib? (even though the proof would kind of need to go through all cases and use general statements)

By Jordan-Holder you only need that every simple group of order <60 is commutative I think?
@Antoine Chambert-Loir
#42890
Oh, I'm only now noticing this
Very funny that we need this for CGT of all things, haha

Do we have all those Sylow-based "no simple group of order pq^2" statements in Mathlib? Or is there a more advanced way to classify simple groups of low order than what I remember from my second-year algebra class?
I don't think so but I'd really love to define a predicate for solvability-forcing numbers (and nilpotency / abelianness / cyclicity)
Ah, I forgot about Burnside's theorem
Do we have it yet?
No but Tau Ceti does

OK, after a short exchange with free Claude, I think we're done up to order 60 by Burnside's theorem + Burnside's p-complement theorem, a corollary of which states that a nonabelian simple group can't have its minimal prime factor have multiplicity 1.

Of course, you can do the elementary Sylow combinatorics + no low index subgroup stuff if you don't want to rely on Burnside
(And on the other hand you could prove the odd order theorem but I don't think that's going to be in Mathlib anytime soon)

you could prove the odd order theorem

I believe there's an AI-generated proof out there. (Of course, this would be nice to have in mathlib, but that will take time.)

Everything we're talking about has either been done by AI or is clearly doable by AI - I'm not sure it's a useful standard. The limiting factor isn't even design work (human or AI), it's Mathlib review pace.

Both, I'd say: "any AI formalisation" is still very different from mathlib quality. You'd need to both have written code of mathlib standards, and get it reviewed (and the former can happen before the latter).
Yes, I think we don't disagree
